name: Principia
info: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica is Isaac Newton's Latin work in three books, first published in 1687, which sets out his laws of motion and his law of universal gravitation and a mathematical foundation for classical mechanics.

facts.made: Isaac Newton, who wrote it from 1684 after Edmond Halley's visit; Halley saw it through the press and paid for the first edition at his own financial risk
facts.form: A Latin work in three books, preceded by definitions and the axioms or laws of motion; argued in geometrical propositions, with later editions in 1713 and 1726
facts.where: Copies of the first edition are held by libraries including Cambridge University Library, which has Newton's own annotated copy, and the Huntington Library, which has another copy of his with his notes
facts.known: The laws of motion; the law of universal gravitation; an explanation of Kepler's laws of planetary motion; the Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy; the General Scholium and Hypotheses non fingo; the dispute with Hooke

t: Newton derived Kepler's laws of planetary motion from an inverse square law of force and showed that the law applied across the Solar System, in the moon's motion, the tides, comets and the precession of the equinoxes.
The book began as a nine-page tract sent to Edmond Halley in 1684, grew over about two years of concentrated work, and was published in 1687 at Halley's own expense.
Its mathematics was accepted readily, but a force acting at a distance drew criticism from Huygens and Leibniz, and Newton answered with Hypotheses non fingo.
dyk: Between May 1684 and April 1686 Newton's chemical notebooks have no entries at all, though he had long kept dated notes of his experiments, which suggests that he did very little else for well over a year and a half.
ev: Newton studies colliding bodies and shows, for circular planetary motion, an inverse-square relation of force to distance
Newton sends Halley the nine-page tract De motu corporum in gyrum
The first book is presented to the Royal Society, Hooke makes a priority claim and Pepys gives his imprimatur
The complete Principia is published by Halley
The second edition appears under the editorship of Roger Cotes, with the General Scholium added
The third edition is published, with Rule 4 of the Rules of Reasoning
A new census of owners of the first edition identifies 387 copies

sections.origins:
The Principia grew out of a conversation in January 1684, when Edmond Halley, Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke discussed planetary motion. Hooke claimed to have derived the inverse-square law and all the laws of planetary motion but produced no derivation. Halley could derive the inverse-square law only for the circular case, and resolved to ask Newton. In August 1684, probably, Newton told him that he had made the derivation some time before but could not find the papers.

Newton's earlier work lay behind this. In the 1660s he studied colliding bodies and showed, for circular planetary motion, that the force had an inverse-square relation with distance from the centre. The work followed Copernicus's heliocentric theory of 1543, Kepler's three laws, Galileo's work on inertia and uniformly accelerated motion, and Descartes's Principia philosophiae of 1644, which held that bodies act on each other only through contact and led to the idea of an aether. A correspondence with Hooke in 1679 and 1680 and a comet seen in the winter of 1680 to 1681 renewed Newton's interest in astronomy.
sections.content:
The Principia opens with definitions and the axioms or laws of motion, and continues in three books. Newton defined mass as the quantity of matter arising from density and magnitude, used it to define the quantity of motion, now called momentum, and treated space and time as absolute, distinguishing them from relative measures taken from perceptible objects. Book 1, subtitled De motu corporum, treats motion without a resisting medium. It begins with lemmas on the method of first and last ratios, a geometrical form of infinitesimal calculus, links centripetal forces to the law of areas and to orbits of conic-section form, and includes the shell theorem and a first study of the three-body problem.

Book 2 concerns motion through resisting media and makes Newton a pioneer of fluid mechanics. Book 3, De mundi systemate, applies the earlier results to the Solar System. It shows stepwise, beginning with the satellites of Jupiter, that the inverse-square law of mutual gravitation holds universally. It treats the irregularities of the moon's motion, comets, the tides and the precession of the equinoxes, and gives estimates of the relative masses of the giant planets, the Earth and the Sun.
sections.making:
Newton sent Halley a nine-page manuscript, De motu corporum in gyrum, in November 1684. It derived Kepler's three laws from an inverse-square force and generalised the result to conic sections. Halley was so excited by it that he went to Newton again in November 1684 to ask for more, and Newton worked in concentrated fashion until at least mid-1686. His secretary Humphrey Newton later recalled that he sometimes forgot his food or sleep, and that he would rush back from his garden to write down a new thought.

Newton first conceived the work as two volumes and wrote a fair copy of a second volume, De motu corporum, Liber Secundus, in about the summer of 1685. He then started afresh in a tighter and less accessible mathematical style, which became Book 3. By his own account he had composed it first in a popular method, and recast it in propositions to prevent disputes with readers who could not lay aside their prejudices. Book 1 had meanwhile grown so much that he divided it in two, which is why the book on the system of the world is Book 3.

Book 1 was presented to the Royal Society at the end of April 1686. Hooke's priority claim led Newton, who hated disputes, to threaten to withdraw Book 3, and Halley tactfully persuaded him not to. Halley bore the cost of publication, and the book appeared in 1687.
sections.reception:
The mathematical parts of the first two books were so clearly consistent that they were easily accepted. John Locke asked Christiaan Huygens whether he could trust the proofs and was assured of their correctness. The idea of an attractive force acting at a distance received a cooler response. Huygens and Leibniz noted that the law was incompatible with the notion of an aether, and from a Cartesian point of view it was a faulty theory. Newton replied that the mathematical form of the theory had to be correct because it explained the data, and he refused to speculate on the nature of gravity. The number of phenomena that the theory organised impressed younger philosophers, who soon adopted the methods and language of the Principia.

In response to criticism that he had introduced occult agencies, Newton added the General Scholium to the second edition of 1713 and wrote there Hypotheses non fingo, that he formulated no hypotheses. In the same text he criticised Descartes's vortex theory and inferred the existence of a god from the system of the world. It has been suggested that this gave an oblique argument for a unitarian conception of God. Later writers praised the book. Clairaut wrote in 1747 that it marked the epoch of a great revolution in physics, and Lagrange called it the greatest production of the human mind.
sections.survival:
The first edition was probably printed in about 500 copies, though estimates have been higher. A survey published in 1953 located 189 surviving copies, and a 2020 study counted 387 owners' copies. It suggests a wider initial readership and a greater early influence on Enlightenment science than had been assumed. Cambridge University Library holds Newton's own copy of the first edition, interleaved with blank pages for his corrections. The Huntington Library has another of his copies, with annotations in his hand. The Bodmer Library in Switzerland keeps a copy once owned by Leibniz, with his notes on the dispute over who first formulated calculus. A first edition at Uppsala University Library was stolen in the 1960s and returned in 2009.

Newton had been urged since the early 1690s to prepare a new edition because copies had grown rare and costly. Richard Bentley arranged the second edition and appointed Roger Cotes as editor, who announced its publication on 30 June 1713. Newton gave no acknowledgement to Cotes, and omitted others, John Flamsteed above all, because of priority disputes. The third edition was published on 25 March 1726 under Henry Pemberton, and the second edition was the basis of the first edition printed abroad, at Amsterdam in 1714.
sections.legacy:
Four full English translations have been made from the third edition. The first, by Andrew Motte in 1729, was the basis of a modernised version of 1934 under Florian Cajori's name. I. Bernard Cohen, Anne Whitman and Julia Budenz published a new translation in 1999, after Cohen criticised the 1934 version. Charles Leedham-Green published another with Cambridge University Press in 2021. In 1739 to 1742 two Minim priests, Thomas LeSeur and François Jacquier, produced an annotated edition, often called the Jesuit edition, which was reprinted more than once in Scotland in the 19th century. Émilie du Châtelet translated all three books into French, with a commentary that applied calculus to Newton's most controversial theories, and hers remains the standard French translation.

The sequence of definitions in the Principia is recognisable in many textbooks today, and its four Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy have been described as the basis of modern approaches to science. In 1977 the Voyager spacecraft carried a picture of a page of the Principia on the Golden Record, and in 2014 the astronaut Tim Peake named his mission to the International Space Station Principia after the book.

summary: The Principia is Isaac Newton's Latin work of 1687 on the mathematical principles of natural philosophy, setting out his laws of motion and law of universal gravitation. Prompted by Edmond Halley and published at his expense, it was revised in 1713 and 1726 and translated many times.
notes: The article gives the imprimatur by Samuel Pepys as 5 July 1686 in its lead and as 30 June 1686 in the section on Halley as publisher; the text and events say 1686 only.

Print run of the first edition: the article gives as many as 750 estimated, then 189 and about 200 further copies located, then 387 owners in a 2020 study, then Macomber's 500 as likely correct. The text says probably about 500 though estimates have been higher, and gives 189 and 387 attributed.

The article says that Hooke 'agreed' that the demonstration of the curves was wholly Newton's, and that Newton denied owing the inverse square law to Hooke; the text mentions only the claim and Newton's reply to Hooke's priority claim in the making section.
The article does not date du Châtelet's translation, so no year is given for it.
'Start' is 1684 for composition begun after Halley's visit; the article says the concentrated work lasted at least until mid-1686.
Left out: the 2016 sale price, the list of other libraries, Varia details beyond Voyager and Peake, calendar of Book 2's correctness claims.
